title: Nubia's churches
hook: Christian kingdoms once flourished on the Nile in what is now Sudan, and their churches were almost forgotten

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lalibela, where churches were carved down into solid rock. Your line was churches in the rock.

Sand, blown over the ruins of a town by the Nile. Archaeologists dig, and under the sand they find walls, and on the walls, faces. Saints with large dark eyes. Angels. Mary holding her child. A bishop in his robes, looking straight out at them as if he'd been waiting. These are the walls of a cathedral at Faras, in old Nubia, the land along the Nile south of Egypt. Whole Christian kingdoms once lived here, and their names had mostly faded from memory.

The Bible already knows this land, though it calls it Ethiopia, its word for the country south of Egypt. A Psalm says, in the King James Bible, "Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God." And in Acts, Philip meets on the road "a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians." He's reading Isaiah; he asks to be baptized, and goes on his way rejoicing. Some readers place his queen's kingdom in the land later called Nubia. Later, kings along the Nile became Christian. Their kingdoms, Nobadia, Makuria and Alodia, built churches and cathedrals, with bishops, monasteries and walls covered in paintings. They worshiped in Greek and Coptic, and wrote in their own Nubian language too. For a long time they flourished. Then, slowly, the kingdoms weakened and the churches emptied. There was no single dramatic fall, the way there was at Constantinople. The faith faded out of the valley, and sand covered the walls. Christian history isn't only Rome, Constantinople and the cathedrals of Europe. It reached Africa early, riding home with that traveler from Philip's road, and it grew along the Nile. This week ran from Jan Hus seeking the truth, through Thomas à Kempis in his nook, Joan's humble answer, the last liturgy, Gutenberg's letters and the rock churches of Lalibela, to faces under the sand. To remember a church is to say: these people were here, and they prayed.

Say the kingdoms' names slowly, once each, Nobadia, Makuria, Alodia, and then the town, Faras. Picture the painted bishop on the wall, the saints with their wide eyes, and the people who once stood before them on an ordinary morning; you don't know their names, but you can hold them for a minute anyway. If you pray, give thanks for them; if you don't, let the names be enough.
Nubia's churches. The churches of the Christian kingdoms on the Nile, in what is now Sudan, which faded and were found again under the sand.
Your line: remembered churches. A name said aloud is a name remembered. Eight hundred forty days now.

howItsDone: The Nubian churches no longer hold services, but paintings from the cathedral at Faras are kept in museums, and Christians in Sudan and elsewhere sometimes remember the Nubian kingdoms as part of their own story.

options: Not at all. It reached Africa early; Christian kingdoms once flourished along the Nile.
Mostly. Before that, Africa's only Christians were a few traders in port towns.

notes: Claims rule: the outline hook's 'eight hundred years' is not stated; no dates are given. Confirm.
'Some readers place his queen's kingdom in the land later called Nubia': Candace (Kandake) as the title of queens of Kush/Meroë; attributed to 'some readers'. Confirm.
Nobadia, Makuria, Alodia; worship in Greek and Coptic with Old Nubian writing; slow decline rather than a single conquest: confirm the summary.
Faras cathedral paintings (saints, angels, Mary, bishops) found under sand; now in museums (Warsaw and Khartoum). Confirm.
'It was African from the start' rests on Acts 8; confirm phrasing is fair and not an overclaim.
